title: Xylophone
summary: Bar-S1 slice: one three-dimensional rosewood bar with a designed undercut (tuned from its own modes so the second mode is three times the first, scaled to the Db5 fundamental, never from a recording), struck by a Hertz silicone sphere and heard at a modal Burton-Miller receiver one metre away. The first render is lossless and only a diagnostic; a second render damps the five elastic modes with a rosewood decay law measured on another bar. There is no resonator, no cord suspension, and no marimba or vibraphone.
physics_present: Quadratic tetrahedral elasticity of the bar with an orthotropic wood scenario, modal analysis of the free-free body and six rigid modes
Burton-Miller boundary-element radiation transfer of the five retained elastic modes to a receiver at one metre
Material Hertz mallet contact with a silicone head, time-stepped with a measured substep ladder
Mode damping from the decay law measured on a rosewood xylophone bar (Chaigne and Doutaut 1997), used as a declared scenario
physics_missing: Wood loss measured on this bar: the decay law belongs to another rosewood bar, and the first render has no loss at all
Transverse rosewood constants and density are scenario values, not measurements of a rosewood bar
Mallet head loss, mallet shaft and the real mallet of the recording
The cord suspension and the bar supports
A tubular resonator below the bar, which a marimba needs and which also changes a xylophone
Only five elastic modes are retained, so partials above a few kHz are absent

Marimba: blocked. The only tabulated instrument found (a home-built padouk marimba by La Favre) gives each bar's arch length and centre thickness but not the arch curve, and a pre-registered check failed: a parabolic arch does not reproduce the 1:4 and 1:10 tuning that the builder states for three of four bars. The Iowa marimba is a rosewood instrument, a different species and maker. The vibraphone has no recording to compare with
